newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC puts substance on free trade vision.
newsitem.headline: APEC puts substance on free trade vision.

text.p: APEC leaders have started to add substance to their vision of free trade around the Pacific Rim by 2020. The question is how much.
The fourth annual summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum ended on Monday on an upbeat note.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, on a re-election high, was delighted with the outcome after reluctant fellow leaders switched signals and agreed to give substantial backing to an American quest to eliminate global tariffs on information technology.
The final summit statement from the leaders of the 18 APEC members expressed their confidence the APEC process "will produce substantial, concrete, measurable and sustainable results".
These would "tangibly improve the lives of all our citizens by the end of the century," said the statement read out by the summit host, Philippine President Fidel Ramos.

The potential is huge, with APEC's 18 member economies accounting for half the world's population and about 56 percent of the world's economic output, and controlling more than 50 percent of global trade.

APEC was conceived in 1989 in Australia, and held its first summit -- hosted by Clinton in Seattle -- four years later. Last year in Osaka a blueprint was presented for an end to tariffs in trade and investment by 2020.
This year the summit approved the Manila Action Plan for APEC (MAPA), taking the first steps to turn the blueprint into reality.

"APEC is not legally binding. If you don't (do) what they say, you'll look very bad. This will show how peer pressure works," former Philippine finance minister Jesus Estanislao was quoted as saying in an interview released by the University of Asia and the Pacific.
Other analysts question the ability of such a diverse group as APEC to progress.
"The APEC process itself is almost geared to under-achievement," a European diplomatic source said.
"The fact that you've got 18 totally different economies making voluntary contributions essentially means that you move at the speed of your slowest member," he said.
Some analysts also asked how APEC would sell itself to its myriad peoples as it moved from grandiose "headline visions" to the nuts and bolts of economic cooperation.

"After Manila, there seems very little else to talk about at the next APEC meeting unless APEC begins extending its agenda beyond trade and investment to include security and geopolitical concerns, new visions to develop," said political analyst Alex Magno.
"The Asian countries are pretty strict on maintaining a straight and narrow path for APEC, but that path might end in Manila," he added.
Critics of APEC have also accused it of being a combination of big government and big business, with little regard for the man in the street -- or the paddy field.

Ramos pushed the "human face" of APEC during the 1996 conference. The summit statement referred to the "human face of development", and a key element of the plan of action is economic and technical cooperation.
APEC's aim, Ramos told a post-summit news conference, "is to create a bigger and bigger pie to divide".
